label: AQ 0032
title: The score that only went down

questions.q: Why not use cross-validation inside the loop instead?
questions.a: It makes each score less noisy, but the loop still chooses by those scores. Dwork et al. note that neither cross-validation nor the bootstrap (rescoring on resampled copies of the data) fixes overfitting to the held-out set in their coin-flip experiment. You still need a test set used once.

questions.q: How would you redesign the overnight loop?
questions.a: First, guard the scorer: before every score, the loop compares the scoring code and the validation data with a hash stored at round 1 and halts on a mismatch, so an edit to the loss-averaging formula can't quietly change the score. The keep bar becomes the baseline's seed spread, not zero. Every 20 rounds or so (our choice) the best gets a full-length run, and the night closes with a single test-split score.

teach.title: How it works: four checks, cheapest first

questions.q: The winner's test score is worse than its validation score. Was the night wasted?
questions.a: Not necessarily: some drop is expected after selecting on validation. Compare the winner with the starting baseline on that test set. If it still wins by more than seed noise, the gain is real, just smaller (our reasoning).

teach.title: How it works: four checks, cheapest first

questions.q: Why does a keep-only-if-better tuning loop always show a falling kept score?
questions.a: An edit is kept only when it beats the best score so far; otherwise it is undone. So the kept score can only stay level or fall, whatever the edits really did.

questions.q: In Dwork et al.'s coin-flip experiment, what did the reused held-out set report, and what was the true accuracy?
questions.a: Over 63% with 500 selected features, on both training and holdout data. The true accuracy was 50%, because the labels were random.

teach.title: How it works: four checks, cheapest first

questions.q: Name four checks before trusting the winner of an overnight agent tuning loop.
questions.a: The scoring code and data are untouched; the gain beats seed-to-seed noise; it holds on a test set scored once; it holds when retrained at the full training length.
